lessons.title: Create your first Claude Project and load it with real documents
lessons.summary: Set up a Claude Project, upload a mix of PDFs, docs and pasted text as project knowledge, and confirm Claude can actually see them before you ask a single question.
lessons.goal: Create a Project in Claude and add at least three real documents of different types so it has grounded material to answer from.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude Projects work because a chat inside the project starts with your uploaded files already in context — every reply can draw on them without you repasting anything. That's different from a one-off chat where you paste a document and it's gone once the conversation ends. But a Project only helps if you deliberately build its file set first: wrong, missing, or unreadable uploads still let Claude answer fluently on the topic from general knowledge, so you can't easily tell whether it actually used your documents unless you check.
steps: Sign into claude.ai on a Pro plan or higher — Projects requires Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise, not the Free tier — and click 'Projects,' then 'Create project.' Decide up front what single topic, client, or case this specific Project represents — each Project is its own workspace with separate files and chat history.

Add your first file through 'Add content' into the project's knowledge. Claude accepts PDFs, Word documents, Excel and CSV files, images, and plain text — pick whatever real document you actually need answers from.

Add at least two more files of different types (for example a PDF plus a spreadsheet plus a pasted block of text) so you can see how Claude handles each format. Keep the per-chat cap in mind: 20 files, 30MB each.

Set custom instructions for the Project — a short note telling Claude what this project is for and to answer only from the uploaded files unless you say otherwise. This isn't automatic the way a source-locked tool would be; Claude will blend in general knowledge unless you explicitly restrict it.

Open a new chat inside the Project and ask Claude to list what it can actually see in project knowledge, confirming every file you uploaded is readable rather than assuming a successful upload means usable text.
Watch specifically for scanned, image-only PDFs — they can upload successfully but yield little to no extractable text, and Claude won't necessarily flag this on its own unless you ask.

Rename any file with a generic name (like 'Document1.pdf') before uploading, or note its real title in your prompt, since Claude doesn't auto-generate a summary per file the way a dedicated document tool would.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable prompt (paste into a new chat inside the Project)
lessons.prompt:
Using only the files currently in this project's knowledge, give me:
1. A one-paragraph overview of what these documents cover as a set.
2. A one-line summary of what each individual file specifically contributes, by file name.
3. Any obvious gaps — topics you'd expect this set of documents to cover but that none of them actually address.
Do not use outside knowledge. If a file seems to have failed to upload properly or you can't extract meaningful text from it, say so explicitly.
lessons.explanation: This prompt is an inventory check, not a real question — it forces Claude to account for every file individually, which immediately surfaces a file that failed to parse (common with scanned PDFs that have no selectable text layer) or one that's redundant with another. Running this before your first real question turns a silent upload failure into something you catch in minute two instead of an hour later.
lessons.example:
Input: a Project with a 40-page PDF policy manual, an onboarding Word document, and a pasted block of text from a company handbook page, plus custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge.

Output: a paragraph noting the set covers employee policy from three angles — a full manual, an onboarding-specific doc, and a handbook excerpt — followed by one line per file on what it uniquely adds, and a flagged gap such as 'none of these files mention remote-work equipment stipends.'
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, create one new Project for a real project or topic you're currently working on, add at least three files of different types plus custom instructions restricting Claude to that content, and run the prompt above.
lessons.expectedResult: You have a Project with three or more files, custom instructions in place restricting Claude to project knowledge, and a completed inventory response confirming what each file contributes and flagging any gaps.
commonMistakes: Uploading scanned or image-only PDFs and assuming Claude extracted the full text just because the upload succeeded.
Skipping custom instructions, so Claude quietly blends general knowledge in with the uploaded material instead of sticking to it.
Dumping unrelated documents into one Project because it's convenient, which muddies every future answer with irrelevant context.
Leaving generic auto-generated filenames in place, making it hard to tell files apart once the Project grows.
lessons.proTip: Turn on Claude's web search only when you actually want outside context blended in deliberately, and say so explicitly in that prompt — project knowledge alone doesn't put Claude into a grounding-only mode the way a dedicated source-locked tool would.

lessons.title: Ask grounded questions in a Claude Project and verify every quoted source yourself
lessons.summary: Query your Project's files, require Claude to quote its sources directly with a file and page reference, then open the original document yourself to check every claim — since Claude has no automatic citation panel to click.
lessons.goal: Ask a substantive question of a real Project and personally verify at least three quoted claims against the original file text to confirm the answer is accurate.
lessons.whyItMatters: Unlike a dedicated source-grounded research tool, Claude doesn't attach clickable citation chips to its answers — there's no side panel that auto-highlights the exact passage a claim came from. That means the trust mechanism has to be a prompting habit you build yourself: explicitly requiring verbatim quotes with a named file and section, then opening that file and checking the quote by hand. Skipping this step throws away the one thing that makes a document-grounded answer more reliable than an ordinary chat reply.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Claude Project from the previous lesson with at least three uploaded files and custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge.
steps: Open a chat inside the Project and ask one specific, answerable question rather than something broad like 'summarize everything.'

In the same prompt, explicitly require Claude to quote the exact sentence or line supporting each claim, plus which file — and page or section, if visible — it came from. Claude will not do this by default.
Open the original file yourself, in the Project's file panel or your own copy, and search for the quoted text to confirm it's accurate and not a paraphrase presented as a quote.
Ask a follow-up question that requires connecting two different files, and confirm the quotes in the new answer actually come from both files, not just one.

Deliberately ask something your files don't cover, and check whether Claude says so plainly or fills the gap with general knowledge — this is the real test of whether your custom instructions are actually holding.

If your plan gives you a model picker, note which model answered — Opus and Sonnet models tend to handle nuanced document questions more carefully than Haiku, which matters if you switch models mid-project.
Remember Claude has no persistent per-file citation record the way a dedicated grounded-research tool does — if you'll need this exact quote again next week, save it somewhere outside the chat.
lessons.prompt:
Answer the following question using only the files in this project's knowledge: [YOUR QUESTION]

For every factual claim, quote the exact sentence it's based on, word for word, and name the file — and page or section, if you can tell — it came from. If the files only partially answer the question, say explicitly what's missing instead of filling the gap with outside knowledge.
lessons.explanation: This prompt does the job a citation-chip panel would do automatically in a dedicated tool — Claude has no built-in click-to-verify UI for project files, so requiring verbatim quotes with a named source is the only way to make an answer auditable. That distinction matters most the moment you're about to repeat the answer to someone else.
lessons.example: Project: an HR policy manual (Word), an onboarding doc, and a benefits PDF, with custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge. Question: 'What is our parental leave policy for part-time employees?' Answer quotes a specific sentence from the benefits PDF and names the file. Opening that PDF confirms the quote is exact. A follow-up question connecting leave policy to PTO accrual pulls quotes from both the manual and the benefits PDF. A test question about a country not covered by any file returns 'the project files don't address this' instead of a guess.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, ask a real question of the Project you built in the previous lesson, then personally open at least three source files to check the quotes Claude gave you.
lessons.expectedResult: You've asked at least one grounded question, personally verified three or more quotes against the original files, confirmed they match what Claude claimed, and tested one question your files don't actually cover.
commonMistakes: Trusting a fluent answer without ever opening a source file to check a quote.
Forgetting to set custom instructions on a new chat, so Claude quietly reverts to blending in general knowledge.
Asking vague, compound questions that produce vague answers with no real quotes attached.
Treating a paraphrase Claude gives you as an exact quote when you're about to repeat it in an official document or to a client.
lessons.proTip: For anything you'll quote externally — a client deliverable, a report, a citation in a legal filing — always open the source file and copy the exact wording yourself rather than trusting Claude's paraphrase verbatim; there's no automatic passage-highlighting to lean on instead.

lessons.title: Synthesize findings across multiple documents in a Claude Project
lessons.summary: Get Claude to structure a cross-document synthesis around agreement, disagreement, and unique points, with a quote and file name on every claim, instead of blending everything into one confident-sounding blur.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured synthesis of four or more related documents uploaded to a Claude Project that clearly separates what files agree on, disagree on, and each contribute uniquely.
lessons.whyItMatters: Professionals who read multiple vendor proposals, research reports, or interview notes on the same question waste hours manually cross-referencing them. A well-structured synthesis prompt turns that into minutes — but only if you explicitly ask for agreement, disagreement, and unique points with a quote and file name on every claim, since a lazy 'summarize all of this' prompt tends to blend documents into one voice and can silently average conflicting numbers.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Claude Project with four or more files covering the same topic from different angles — for example several vendor proposals, competitor reports, or candidate profiles — plus custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge.
steps: Upload several files to one Project that genuinely overlap on the same topic, not just loosely related documents.
Ask a broad synthesis question first, and notice whether the answer distinguishes files or blends them into one voice — this is a useful diagnostic on its own.
Re-ask with an explicit structure request: points of agreement, points of disagreement, and points unique to a single file, each with a quote.
Follow up specifically on any numeric claims that differ across files, since numbers are where silent blending, like averaging, causes the most damage.
Cross-check the disagreement section yourself by opening the named files and confirming the quoted figures are accurate.
Ask Claude to reformat the numeric parts of the comparison as a markdown table for a clean side-by-side view you can paste elsewhere.
Save the synthesized answer somewhere outside the chat — a doc or note — so it persists, since a Project's chat history isn't a structured record the way a dedicated saved-notes feature would be.
lessons.prompt:
Compare the files in this project's knowledge on [TOPIC, e.g. pricing, timeline, and scope]. Structure your answer as:
1. Points all files agree on, with a supporting quote and file name for each.
2. Points where files disagree — quote each file's specific claim or figure, with its file name. Do not blend conflicting numbers into an average or pick one as the answer.
3. Points that are unique to only one file.
Keep each file's contribution clearly attributed throughout.
lessons.explanation: Forcing an explicit agree/disagree/unique structure, and explicitly forbidding averaging or picking a winner, stops Claude from doing the one thing that makes multi-document synthesis dangerous: silently resolving a real disagreement into a single plausible-sounding number. Requiring a quote and file name on every claim preserves the traceability you need if someone later asks 'where did this come from.'
lessons.example: Three vendor proposal PDFs uploaded to a Project. Output shows pricing differing significantly across all three vendors with per-file quotes and names, agreement that implementation takes roughly six weeks, and one vendor uniquely offering a feature the other two didn't mention at all.
lessons.exercise: Upload four or more real overlapping documents to a Project — competitor reports, candidate materials, or vendor proposals — and run the structured synthesis prompt. Ask for a markdown table if any part of the comparison is numeric.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured synthesis that clearly separates agreement, disagreement, and unique points, with every claim backed by a quote and a named file, and no numbers silently averaged or blended.
commonMistakes: Asking a vague 'summarize all of this' prompt that blends files into one voice, losing track of which file said what.
Ignoring flagged disagreements because the overall summary reads confidently and smoothly.
Not verifying numeric claims against the named file before repeating them in a decision or recommendation.
Assuming the majority view across files is automatically the correct one without weighing source quality or recency.
lessons.proTip: Ask Claude to turn the finished synthesis into a downloadable Artifact — a formatted comparison document — so you have something clean to hand off, instead of chat text you'd have to reformat yourself.

lessons.title: Turn a course's readings and slides into a study system with Gemini
lessons.summary: Upload your actual slides and readings into Gemini, then prompt it to generate a study guide, flashcard-style practice questions, and a concept map you can check against the real material.
lessons.goal: Generate a full study set from real course materials uploaded to Gemini, and use at least two targeted follow-up prompts to fix weak spots practice questions revealed.
lessons.whyItMatters: Exam prep from scattered PDFs and slide decks is slow, and generic study apps aren't grounded in what your specific course actually assigned. Gemini's file upload takes PDFs, Google Docs, Slides, and images directly, and because coursework so often already lives in Google Docs and Slides, you can frequently pull materials straight from Drive instead of exporting them first. Gemini has no dedicated one-click quiz or flashcard generator, so the study set only stays grounded if you explicitly restrict every prompt to the uploaded material and check the output against your real readings.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Real materials for one course unit or module — lecture slides, assigned readings, and your own notes — ready to upload to Gemini as files or pulled from Drive.
steps: Start one Gemini conversation per course unit or module, not per whole course or semester, so generated study material stays scoped to what's actually being tested next.
Upload lecture slides (PDF or straight from Google Slides), assigned readings, and your own lecture notes pasted in as text, directly in the chat.
Ask Gemini to generate a study guide from only the uploaded material, then skim it against your sources — check that the key concepts and definitions match what was actually assigned.

Ask for a set of flashcard-style question-and-answer pairs, and spot-check a handful against the real reading — with no built-in review step, an occasional flattened nuance can slip through unnoticed.

Ask for a short practice quiz to self-test. For every missed question, ask Gemini to point to exactly where in the uploaded material it's covered, then go re-read that passage rather than just re-reading the flashcard.
Ask Gemini to sketch how the unit's concepts connect to each other in a short outline, which is often easier to follow than reading slides linearly.

For any concept that keeps tripping you up, use a targeted follow-up prompt asking for a plain-language explanation grounded in the uploaded files, rather than regenerating the whole study guide again.
If your materials already live in Drive, use Gemini's Workspace side panel in Docs to turn the study guide into a clean, shareable document.
lessons.prompt:
I got this practice question wrong: [PASTE THE QUESTION AND YOUR WRONG ANSWER]

Using only the course materials I uploaded in this conversation, explain the correct answer in plain language, point to exactly where in the uploaded material this is covered, and give me one new, different question that tests whether I actually understand it now — not the same question reworded.
lessons.explanation: This targets the specific gap the practice quiz just revealed instead of regenerating a generic summary you'll skim past. Asking Gemini to point to exactly where the material covers it forces you back to the real reading rather than trusting a possibly-imprecise generated flashcard, and asking for a genuinely new follow-up question checks understanding instead of pattern-matched recall.
lessons.example: A biology unit uploaded as two chapter PDFs and a Slides deck exported to PDF. A flashcard-style question on 'mitochondria vs. chloroplast function' gets answered wrong. The prompt returns a corrected explanation pointing to chapter 4, page 12, plus a new differentiating question that can't be answered by just memorizing the original card.
lessons.exercise: Upload a real course-unit's materials to Gemini, generate a study guide, flashcard-style Q&A pairs, and a practice quiz, then run the follow-up prompt on at least two questions you got wrong.
lessons.expectedResult: A full generated study set built from your actual course materials, plus at least two targeted remediation exchanges where you verified the correct answer's location in the material and answered a genuinely new follow-up question correctly.
commonMistakes: Uploading an entire semester's materials into one conversation, so generated quizzes and study guides mix content from unrelated units.
Trusting generated flashcards or quiz questions without spot-checking a sample against the actual reading.
Using generated study material as the only prep instead of still engaging with the primary sources for what's actually likely to be tested.
Re-reading the same flashcard after missing a practice question instead of asking Gemini exactly where in the material it's covered.
lessons.proTip: Teachers can build one grounded study set per unit and share it as a Google Doc through the Workspace side panel, instead of asking every student to upload the same materials and regenerate the same study guide individually.

lessons.title: Turn a stack of work documents into a briefing you can hand to your team with Claude
lessons.summary: Upload meeting transcripts, reports, and notes to a Claude Project, then produce a decision-ready briefing with a scoped, audience-specific prompt and a quoted evidence trail for every material fact.
lessons.goal: Produce a short, audience-scoped briefing in Claude where every material fact traces to a quoted source, ready to hand to stakeholders.
lessons.whyItMatters: Professionals routinely spend hours condensing meeting notes, reports, and emails into a briefing for people who won't read the source material themselves. Claude's project knowledge plus a well-scoped prompt can produce something citable — and defensible if someone asks where a number came from — in minutes instead of hours. But Claude has no automatic grounding guarantee the way a source-locked tool does; it will happily blend in plausible-sounding context unless you explicitly restrict it and require quotes.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Claude Project with real work sources behind a current decision or update — meeting transcripts, a report, and relevant emails or notes pasted in as text — plus custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge.
steps: Gather the actual materials behind a real decision or update into one Project: meeting transcripts, a report, and any related notes or emails.
Ask Claude for a first-draft briefing and review its structure against what you actually need to communicate — a first pass usually reads too much like a general recap.
Refine it with a scoped prompt that names the specific audience and what they need to decide or do — a generic summary is not the same as a decision brief.
Check that every recommendation or claim in the output has a supporting quote and a named file, since you need to be able to answer 'where did this come from' if leadership asks.
Trim the output to what the audience actually needs — a briefing is not a re-summary of everything in the Project.
Ask Claude to render the final version as an Artifact — a clean, formatted document you can edit in place and export, instead of chat text you'd have to reformat yourself.
Paste or export the final briefing into whatever doc or email tool your team actually uses — the Project is where you build it, not necessarily where your team reads it.
lessons.prompt:
Write a briefing for [AUDIENCE, e.g. our leadership team] about [TOPIC OR DECISION], based only on the files in this project's knowledge. Include:
1. The situation in 2-3 sentences.
2. The 3-5 most important facts they need, each with a supporting quote and the file it came from.
3. What decision or action is being requested, if any.
4. Open questions the files don't resolve.
Keep it under [LENGTH]. Do not add outside context or recommendations that aren't supported by these files.
lessons.explanation: Naming the audience and the action needed forces a decision brief rather than a generic recap. Requiring a quote and named source on every fact, and explicitly forbidding outside context, guards against Claude padding gaps with plausible-sounding but unsourced claims — which matters most exactly when the output is headed to people who will act on it without checking the source files themselves.
lessons.example: A Project with three meeting transcripts and a vendor report about a system migration. Output: a 3-sentence situation summary, four quoted facts covering cost, timeline, risk, and vendor readiness with the source file named for each, a clear line reading 'decision requested: approve budget by [date],' and one open question flagged as unresolved in the files.
lessons.exercise: Upload the real supporting documents behind a current work decision to a Claude Project, generate the briefing, refine it with the prompt above, and verify every fact's quote before sending it anywhere.
lessons.expectedResult: A short, audience-scoped briefing where every material fact is traceable to a quoted, named source, with open questions clearly flagged and no unsupported additions.
commonMistakes: Letting the briefing balloon into a full re-summary of every file instead of only what the specific audience needs to act on.
Skipping quote verification on numbers that will get repeated in a meeting or forwarded externally.
Using Claude's first-draft briefing as final output without editing tone and framing for the actual audience.
Including tangential materials in the Project that dilute the briefing instead of sharpening it.
lessons.proTip: Keep the 'open questions the files don't resolve' section in every briefing — it's often more useful to a stakeholder than the summary itself, because it tells them exactly what still needs to be found out.

lessons.title: Maintain a living client or project knowledge base in a Claude Project
lessons.summary: Set up and actively maintain a persistent per-client or per-project Claude Project that stays accurate as documents pile up and versions change over weeks or months.
lessons.goal: Build or update a real client or project Claude Project with a clear file-versioning convention, and run a verified meeting-prep prompt from it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Consultants, lawyers, and freelancers juggle multiple clients, each generating a growing trail of engagement letters, drafts, correspondence, and deliverables. A maintained per-client Project prevents re-reading everything before each meeting and reduces the real risk of citing an outdated draft in front of the client whose deadline depends on it. Claude's memory feature can carry some cross-session continuity, but the project knowledge files are still what actually grounds an answer — a manually maintained recap file matters more than relying on memory alone.
lessons.beforeYouStart: An ongoing real client engagement or project with multiple documents, or a realistic proxy if you're practicing.
steps: Decide the Project boundary before adding anything: one Project per client or per project, never one shared Project across multiple clients — mixing them risks Claude blending context between engagements in an answer, which matters especially for confidentiality-sensitive work.

Establish a naming convention for files — date-stamp meeting notes, label draft versions clearly (v1, v2, final) — so it's obvious which document is currently authoritative, since Claude has no built-in version-supersession feature.

Add a standing recap file you personally maintain and update by hand, and set custom instructions telling Claude to treat it as the current source of truth. A manually curated status file is what actually keeps a Project's grounded answers accurate across weeks, more than Claude's own memory of past chats.
Set a cadence for adding new files as the engagement progresses: each new deliverable, call transcript, or revised contract goes in as it's created, not in a batch months later.
Periodically remove or clearly supersede outdated files so grounded answers don't quote a stale draft — watch your plan's project-knowledge limits if a long engagement's file set grows large.
Before each client meeting, run a standing prep prompt against the Project instead of manually re-reading everything.

Be deliberate about what you upload. Client data lives inside your Claude account under this Project, so check your firm's confidentiality and data-handling policy — including your plan's data-retention settings — before uploading sensitive material.
lessons.prompt:
This is a client knowledge base for [CLIENT OR PROJECT NAME]. Using only the files currently in this project's knowledge, prepare me for [UPCOMING MEETING OR CALL] by giving me:
1. The current status of every open item, with a supporting quote and file name.
2. Anything that changed since the last version of [SPECIFIC DOCUMENT, e.g. the SOW].
3. Commitments we've made to the client that haven't yet been delivered.
4. Questions I should ask them.
Flag anything that looks contradicted by a more recent file rather than picking one version silently.
lessons.explanation: The change-detection and contradiction-flagging request matters once a Project accumulates multiple versions of the same document over time — without being told to prefer recency and flag conflicts explicitly, Claude may silently answer from whichever version it happens to read first, which is exactly the failure mode a living knowledge base needs to avoid.
lessons.example: A consulting engagement Project with SOW v1 and v2 uploaded as separate files, four call transcripts, and a status report. The prep prompt surfaces that v2 changed the delivery date, but a transcript from last week still references the old date — flagged as a contradiction — plus three open action items, each with a quote and file name.
lessons.exercise: Build or update a real client or project Claude Project, add a manually maintained recap file, and run the meeting-prep prompt before your next real interaction with that client.
lessons.expectedResult: A maintained, single-client Project with a clear file-versioning convention, and one verified meeting-prep output that correctly flagged at least one outdated-versus-current conflict or genuinely open item.
commonMistakes: Mixing multiple clients' documents into one Project, risking context bleeding between engagements in an answer.
Letting superseded drafts pile up next to current versions with no naming convention, so Claude can't tell which is authoritative.
Treating the Project as done after initial setup instead of feeding it new files as the engagement actually progresses.
Uploading sensitive client material without first checking your organization's confidentiality or data-handling policy.
lessons.proTip: For regulated or confidentiality-sensitive work, confirm your organization's data policy — and your Claude plan's data-retention and training settings — before uploading client materials to a Project; grounding quality doesn't change your underlying data-handling obligations.

lessons.title: Compare and reconcile documents that disagree with each other using Claude
lessons.summary: Get Claude to explicitly surface, quote, and categorize conflicting claims across uploaded documents instead of quietly flattening the disagreement into one confident answer.
lessons.goal: Produce a ranked, quoted list of genuine disagreements between documents, correctly categorized by type, and personally verify at least one against the originals.
lessons.whyItMatters: Real work documents legitimately conflict — two contract drafts, two expert opinions, two witness statements, two analysts' forecasts — and deciding which to trust, or how to reconcile them, is exactly the professional judgment call that must not get silently flattened by an AI summary. Surfacing conflict explicitly is a different skill than summarizing, and it needs a deliberately different prompt.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Claude Project with files that contain genuine factual, numeric, or interpretive disagreement — for example two contract drafts, two competing forecasts, or conflicting policy documents — plus custom instructions restricting Claude to project knowledge.
steps: Upload files to the Project that you know disagree on at least one real point — two contract drafts, competing forecasts, or conflicting statements.
Ask a broad question first and notice whether the answer surfaces the conflict unprompted or blends it into one voice — this is a useful diagnostic before you write a real prompt.
Re-ask with an explicit request to surface every point of disagreement, quoting each file's specific wording or number, with the file named for each side.
Ask Claude to categorize each disagreement: a factual or numeric contradiction, a difference in interpretation, or simply a difference in scope or emphasis that isn't a real contradiction at all.
For contract or policy work, ask specifically for clause-level or section-level differences rather than a whole-document comparison.
Cross-check the flagged disagreements yourself by opening both files and confirming Claude isn't misreading one of them.
Document your resolution decision — which file controls, and why — outside the Project, since Claude correctly won't make that judgment call for you.
lessons.prompt:
These files may disagree with each other on [TOPIC OR SECTION]. Do not resolve or average any disagreement yourself. For every point where files conflict:
1. Quote each file's exact claim or figure, and name the file.
2. State plainly whether this is a factual contradiction, a numeric discrepancy, a difference in interpretation, or just a difference in scope or emphasis.
3. Do not tell me which one is correct — that's my call.
List the conflicts in order of how consequential the disagreement looks, most important first.
lessons.explanation: The instruction not to resolve or average is the load-bearing line — asked to simply 'compare these,' Claude will often quietly synthesize one blended answer, hiding exactly the disagreement you need to see. Requiring a quote plus named file on both sides keeps the comparison auditable, and refusing to let Claude declare a winner keeps that judgment call where it actually belongs: with you.
lessons.example: A Project with two vendor contract drafts uploaded as files. The prompt surfaces that draft A's liability cap is $50,000 while draft B's is $250,000 — a numeric contradiction quoted from each clause with the file named — and that draft A's termination notice period is 30 days versus draft B's 60 days, ranked above a lower-stakes wording difference in the definitions section.
lessons.exercise: Upload two real conflicting documents you actually need to reconcile — or a realistic proxy — to a Claude Project and run the reconciliation prompt, verifying at least one flagged conflict by opening both files yourself.
lessons.expectedResult: A ranked list of genuine disagreements between files, each quoted and named from both sides, correctly categorized by type, with no premature resolution — and you've personally verified at least one flagged conflict against the original files.
commonMistakes: Asking a generic 'compare these' question, which tends to quietly blend conflicting files into one plausible-sounding but wrong composite.
Accepting flagged disagreements without opening both files to confirm Claude read them correctly.
Letting Claude pick which file is 'right' instead of treating that as your own professional judgment call.
Confusing a scope or emphasis difference, where both files are correct but talking about different things, with a real contradiction.
lessons.proTip: Rerun the reconciliation prompt any time you add a newer or more authoritative file to the Project, such as a signed final version or an amendment — reconciliation isn't a one-time pass, it needs repeating whenever the file set changes.

lessons.title: Build advanced team knowledge workflows with Gemini and Google Workspace
lessons.summary: Design a repeatable, shared Gemini workflow — ownership, source conventions, a reusable Gem, and Workspace-grounded Deep Research — that a team can rely on, not just one person's ad hoc uploads.
lessons.goal: Build or upgrade one shared team knowledge workflow using Gemini's Workspace-grounded Deep Research and a reusable Gem, with real feedback from at least one teammate.
lessons.whyItMatters: The habits from earlier lessons — good sources, verified quotes, careful reconciliation — don't automatically scale once multiple people rely on the same knowledge for onboarding, recurring meetings, or shared decisions. Gemini's Deep Research can ground a report directly in a team's Gmail, Chat, and Drive content alongside the public web, a genuinely different capability than manually uploading files one at a time — but without clear ownership and conventions, a promising shared workflow still goes stale within weeks.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real team or organizational knowledge need this could support — onboarding, a recurring meeting-notes corpus, or a shared project repository — ideally already living in Google Workspace (Gmail, Docs, Drive).
steps: Pick one real team knowledge problem to pilot rather than trying to boil the ocean: an onboarding packet, a recurring meeting corpus, or a shared research repository.
Decide ownership up front — one person responsible for keeping the relevant Drive folder and any custom Gem current, instead of everyone building their own version of the same thing.

Use Gemini's Deep Research with Workspace sources enabled to pull directly from the team's Gmail, Chat, and Drive content (Docs, Sheets, Slides) alongside the public web, instead of manually collecting and uploading every file by hand.

Create a Gem — a reusable custom persona with standing instructions — for the team's specific knowledge domain, for example a new-hire FAQ assistant scoped to the onboarding folder, so output stays consistent no matter who runs it.
Standardize a small library of reusable prompts for the team — a weekly recap, a new-hire FAQ, a meeting-decision log — built on top of the Gem so nobody has to re-explain context from scratch.

Choose the output format that matches the audience: a Doc for async written updates through the Workspace side panel, a Sheet for structured data, or a short Deep Research report for something that needs broader grounding than one team's files.
Share the Gem and any generated documents with the relevant teammates, and decide deliberately who has edit access to the underlying Drive folder versus view-only access.
Set a review cadence for the shared Gem and its source folder, the same way you'd review a live automation, so stale files get pruned and the team keeps trusting it.
lessons.prompt: We're building a shared [TOPIC, e.g. new-hire onboarding] knowledge workflow for our team. Using Deep Research with our Workspace sources enabled, identify the 10 questions a new team member would most likely ask that our Gmail, Docs, and Drive content can actually answer, and answer each one in 2-3 sentences with the source document named. If there's an obviously important question our current sources don't cover, list it separately as a gap for us to fill rather than guessing an answer.
lessons.explanation: Framing the request as 'questions a new person would ask' produces a genuinely usable FAQ instead of a generic summary nobody rereads. Enabling Workspace sources means Deep Research draws on what the team has actually already written in Gmail and Drive instead of requiring you to manually re-upload it, and the explicit gap-listing instruction turns missing documentation into an actionable task for whoever owns the folder.
lessons.example: An onboarding workflow built from a handbook Doc, a benefits PDF in Drive, and a team-norms Doc, with Workspace sources enabled. Output produces a 10-question FAQ — 'How much PTO do I get in year one?' sourced to the benefits PDF, and so on — plus a flagged gap: 'these sources don't specify who approves expense reports over $500.'
lessons.exercise: Pick one real team knowledge need, set up or upgrade a shared Gem and Drive folder for it, run the standing FAQ prompt with Workspace sources enabled, and share the output with at least one real teammate for feedback.
lessons.expectedResult: A shared, owned Gem with a documented source folder convention, at least one reusable standing prompt producing a sourced FAQ or briefing artifact, an explicitly flagged coverage gap, and real feedback from at least one teammate who actually used it.
commonMistakes: Letting every team member build their own version of the same Gem or document instead of maintaining one canonical, owned version.
Picking an output format for novelty rather than because it's what the actual audience will use.
Sharing a Gem or Doc without agreeing on who's responsible for keeping the underlying Drive folder current, so it goes stale within weeks.
Turning on Deep Research's Workspace sources without checking what it can actually access, and being surprised by what it surfaces.
lessons.proTip: Pilot any new shared workflow against one real recurring need before rolling it out broadly — a knowledge workflow that solves zero real problems for its first audience won't get adopted no matter how good the tooling is.
